summary: The recorded owner is a standalone, nonshipping console renderer profiling command, not an ASP.NET request or circuit. Its supplied normal grid producers introduce no identified incomplete asynchronous operation. The shared CLI async-handler overload itself blocks on Task<int>.Result. A local async-lambda substitution is therefore not an established starvation or performance fix and can change prelude exception behavior. No candidate or product-native correctness experiment is justified by this bounded source evidence.

trace.finding: The executable's void Main calls new Program().Execute(args) synchronously. Program registers exactly one supplied subcommand, new GridScenario(). Execute selects the matching command during parsing, then returns command.Invoke(). Invoke is Func<int>. OnExecute(Func<int>) stores that delegate. OnExecute(Func<Task<int>>) does not make the parser asynchronous: it stores () => invoke().Result. The project compiles the in-tree shared CommandLineUtils source rather than depending on a different external CLI handler contract.
trace.exitBoundary: Main ignores Execute's returned int and has no explicit catch, Environment.Exit or exit-code assignment. No exact native process exit status for a scenario/error was observed or is claimed.

trace.finding: The synchronous handler parses --cycles with InvariantCulture, defaulting to one; builds its service provider; obtains ILoggerFactory; and constructs ConsoleHostRenderer. PopulateServiceCollection adds logging and has no supplied override. The handler then calls ExecuteAsync(renderer,numCycles).Wait(), computes and prints the duration only after that terminal barrier returns, and returns zero. Wait is once per selected CLI invocation, outside the per-cycle loop.

GridScenario defaults to FastGrid and also accepts PlainTable and ComplexTable. Each normal cycle creates a GridRendering root, calls Show, assigns it to the renderer, awaits its first RenderRootComponentAsync, calls ChangePage, and awaits the second root render. GridRendering uses two statically produced arrays of 200 forecasts and 20 listed columns. FastGrid registers columns synchronously in OnInitialized and queues a synchronous extra render from its first OnAfterRender. The table modes only render supplied data and wire event delegates; the console scenario does not dispatch their click events. No supplied asynchronous lifecycle override, timer, Task.Delay, Task.Yield, I/O or deliberately delayed renderer was identified or introduced.

ConsoleHostRenderer is sealed, uses new NullDispatcher(), and returns Task.CompletedTask from UpdateDisplayAsync because there is no display. NullDispatcher.CheckAccess always returns true and its InvokeAsync overloads call work inline or return its task; it does not install a renderer synchronization context or schedule a new worker. The recorded entrypoint does not establish an HTTP/request/circuit owner or a request-thread-pool concurrency producer. Calling an async method does not itself queue that method to the pool. Actual thread IDs, scheduler state and Task completion states were not observed.

trace.finding: RenderRootComponentAsync starts pending-task tracking, supplies real component parameters, and awaits WaitForQuiescence. ComponentState obtains the component's real SetParametersAsync task and passes it to AddToPendingTasksWithErrorHandling. Already successful/cancelled tasks are not added; incomplete tasks are error-handled and tracked. WaitForQuiescence repeatedly awaits the pending Task.WhenAll set until parameter/lifecycle work is quiescent. ComponentBase's default initialization/parameter/after-render tasks and CascadingValue's parameter supply return completed tasks for the supplied synchronous component bodies. This supports a source-level expectation of inline completion on the ordinary success path, not a measured runtime assertion.
trace.importantBoundary: Do not interpret root-render quiescence as waiting for arbitrary asynchronous OnAfterRenderAsync work. ProcessRenderQueue deliberately discards InvokeRenderCompletedCalls' task. OnAfterRender may enqueue further synchronous work, which ProcessRenderQueue drains. The supplied FastGrid after-render action is synchronous; no invented delayed callback is used to turn this distinction into a finding.

trace.finding: GridRendering's after-render notification calls BenchmarkEvent.Send synchronously. BenchmarkEvent explicitly documents the null JS-runtime console environment and null-conditionally invokes an in-process runtime. The console host has no JS-runtime registration or browser/display transport. Its display task is completed rather than a browser acknowledgment. No browser process, JS producer, DOM observable or browser validation was exercised.

One service provider and renderer are created per CLI handler invocation. The scenario assigns a fresh root per cycle and does not remove it. The handler does not explicitly dispose the provider or renderer. The existing terminal barrier precedes output and handler return; replacing it with fire-and-forget would lose that ordering for genuinely incomplete tasks. No lifetime, disposal, cache, root-retention or harness change is proposed or implemented.

ConsoleHostRenderer.HandleException rethrows with ExceptionDispatchInfo. Renderer normalizes synchronous component parameter exceptions into faulted tasks, routes component errors through any applicable error boundary and otherwise invokes this handler. Scenario-task failures reach the outer Wait, whose Task contract aggregates task failures. Prelude failures such as int.Parse occur before that Wait in the current synchronous delegate. Simply changing the delegate to async would capture such prelude failures into Task<int>, and the existing CLI .Result adapter would wrap them instead of preserving the current direct-throw boundary. Task-failure/cancellation wrapper details and native error exits were not executed or verified; no universal equivalence claim is made.

DateTime.Now is sampled after service-provider/logger/renderer construction and immediately before the scenario call; the second sample is after Wait. The interval therefore encloses the scenario's own selection/setup and both root-render calls per cycle, including any synchronous scenario initialization. The handler divides by numCycles and prints one decimal-place milliseconds per cycle. It has no separate warmup in the inspected source. Removing the terminal wait or moving its continuation can change what work/order the interval includes. Measurement code was read, not executed or redesigned.
